Gamma Alert: From Natural-Hazard Alerts to Visible Surface Change

Project Summary

Natural-hazard information is often distributed across scientific catalogs, seismic networks, meteorological platforms, and international monitoring systems. An alert may tell us that an earthquake, flood, cyclone, tsunami, or volcanic event occurred, but it does not always help us understand how close it is, whether it remains relevant, or what may have changed on the ground.

We developed Gamma Alert, a Progressive Web App that transforms Earth observation data and scientific reports into a clear, location-based experience. The platform combines NASA EONET, GIBS, POWER, CMR, NISAR, and Worldview with information from seismic networks, tsunami warning centers, meteorological services, and international disaster-monitoring organizations.

Its central feature is the NISAR Surface Explorer, which searches for radar observations covering a selected location, organizes them by date, and allows users to compare the surface before and after an event. Gamma Alert also provides a multi-hazard map, event history, environmental assessment, safety guidance, background notifications, and a Loved Ones feature that informs users when a trusted contact is near a relevant event.

Our central idea is simple: alerts tell us that something happened; NISAR helps us explore what happened to the surface. By connecting both parts, Gamma Alert makes space-based science more accessible for education, preparedness, family awareness, and community resilience.

The Problem

Earth’s surface is constantly changing. Wetlands expand and contract, vegetation responds to moisture, floods transform landscapes, volcanic environments evolve, and earthquakes can affect the ground and surrounding infrastructure.

NASA and other scientific institutions already collect valuable information about these processes. However, the data is divided among platforms that use different formats, categories, update frequencies, and technical language.

Earthquakes may be published through GeoJSON, RSS, or specialized seismic services. Tsunami centers distribute Atom feeds and Common Alerting Protocol documents. NASA services expose event catalogs, geospatial tiles, climate time series, satellite imagery, radar products, and scientific metadata.

This fragmentation makes it difficult for a general user to answer basic questions. What happened? Where did it happen? How far away is it? Is the report recent? Which institution published it? Can Earth observation data help us examine the affected location?

There is also an important separation between alerts and surface observations. An alert communicates that an event exists, but it does not automatically show how the area appears across different dates. Scientific radar products can provide that additional perspective, but they are rarely presented in a format designed for the general public.

Gamma Alert addresses both challenges. It centralizes natural-hazard information and connects relevant events with an interactive NISAR surface-comparison experience.

Our Solution

Gamma Alert begins with a location. Users can grant access to their current position, restore a previously saved location, or use a demonstration location.

The application sends the coordinates to its internal APIs. The server validates the request and queries several scientific sources in parallel. Their responses are converted into a shared event model containing the hazard category, date, coordinates, severity, magnitude, distance, source, original link, and additional technical details.

Reports that describe the same event are grouped together. Gamma Alert then calculates the distance between each event and the user and applies relevance rules based on hazard type, magnitude, severity, age, and proximity.

The results are divided into current events and historical context. The interface presents them through an interactive map, event cards, source information, environmental analysis, safety guidance, and notifications.

When an event has a location and date that can be studied with radar, the user can continue to the Surface Explorer. Gamma Alert searches for NISAR observations, selects compatible acquisitions, and creates an interactive comparison.

The complete experience follows a clear sequence:

Scientific alert → geographic evaluation → event selection → NISAR search → before-and-after comparison → interpretation and communication

The NISAR Surface Explorer

The NISAR Surface Explorer is the central feature through which Gamma Alert responds to the challenge.

NISAR is an active radar mission developed by NASA and ISRO. Unlike passive optical instruments, radar emits its own microwave signal and measures the energy that returns from Earth’s surface. This allows it to observe during the day, at night, and through cloud cover.

Radar response is influenced by surface roughness, moisture, vegetation structure, geometry, and polarization. These characteristics make NISAR valuable for exploring wetlands, floods, vegetation, soil moisture, volcanic environments, and other forms of surface change.

Gamma Alert queries NASA’s Common Metadata Repository through GET /api/nisar/search. The endpoint receives a geographic point and searches the validated and provisional NISAR Level 2 GCOV collections.

The server validates each returned granule name and extracts its frame, acquisition date, and polarization. Gamma Alert currently selects DHDH products because their public RGB previews contain the HH and HV information used by the interface.

The observations are grouped by frame and date. When both provisional and validated products exist for the same acquisition, the validated product receives priority. The system also favors frames containing at least two dates so that a temporal comparison can be performed.

Gamma Alert retrieves the KML footprint associated with the radar preview, calculates its geographic bounds, and verifies that the selected location falls inside the image. The resulting timeline is then returned to the browser.

Users can select the dates manually. When the Surface Explorer is opened from an event, Gamma Alert attempts to select the final observation before the event and the first available observation after it. The interface displays the number of days between acquisitions and an approximate future orbital opportunity based on NISAR’s repeat cycle.

Browser-Based Radar Comparison

The radar comparison is processed directly in the browser with the Canvas API. Gamma Alert uses public NISAR GCOV preview images instead of downloading the much larger scientific HDF5 products.

The application loads the before and after images, converts them into ImageData, and confirms that they share the same dimensions. The geographic area selected by the user is translated into a common pixel window using the KML-derived frame bounds.

Gamma Alert verifies that both images contain enough usable data inside the selected crop. The HH channel is then smoothed using a five-by-five moving average. This reduces isolated visual variation and emphasizes broader spatial patterns.

Radar previews from different dates may have different overall brightness. To compensate for this, Gamma Alert samples the differences between both images and calculates a median offset. That offset is applied before local changes are classified.

Pixels that remain dark in both observations are excluded from the exploratory comparison. The remaining pixels are evaluated using a visual threshold of 38 on the preview’s 0-to-255 brightness scale.

Pixels with a substantial reduction in brightness are displayed in blue. Pixels with a substantial increase are shown in yellow or orange. The result contains the before image, after image, change mask, geographic crop, number of comparable pixels, and percentages of pixels that became brighter or darker.

Users can explore the original observations through a before-and-after slider and compare them with the generated change mask. NASA Worldview provides complementary optical imagery, helping users relate the radar patterns to a more familiar view of the landscape.

Understanding the Radar Results

Radar imagery is more than a conventional photograph. A dark area may represent open water or another smooth surface that reflects the radar signal away from the sensor. A brighter area may be associated with rougher terrain, increased moisture, structured vegetation, buildings, or double-bounce scattering.

The preview’s red and blue channels represent HH information, while the green channel represents HV. HH is currently used for the change calculation. HV contributes useful visual information about vegetation and volumetric scattering.

The comparison is designed as an exploratory visualization. The percentages describe apparent brightness changes among comparable pixels. They do not independently confirm damage, flooding, or the cause of the observed difference.

Gamma Alert therefore presents the acquisition dates, source product, polarization information, geographic context, and interpretation guidance together. This helps users understand both the value of the observations and the scientific care required when interpreting them.

Prepared Study Areas

Gamma Alert contains prepared NISAR acquisition series for four locations in Costa Rica: Palo Verde, Caño Negro, Rincón de la Vieja, and Tortuguero.

Palo Verde and Caño Negro provide opportunities to explore wetlands, water, vegetation, and seasonal surface conditions. Rincón de la Vieja provides a volcanic and mountainous environment where roughness, moisture, vegetation, and terrain geometry can influence radar response. Tortuguero provides a coastal and tropical landscape with water, wetlands, and dense vegetation.

Each study area includes its geographic bounds, radar timeline, acquisition status, and explanatory context. Users can select different dates, inspect the original previews, and generate their own comparison.

These prepared locations make the Surface Explorer usable during a demonstration even when the user is not familiar with NISAR product discovery. The same interface can also search for observations covering other compatible locations.

Multi-Hazard Event Engine

Gamma Alert’s main dashboard uses GET /api/events to retrieve current and historical natural events.

The server queries NASA EONET, GDACS, PTWC, NTWC, the National Hurricane Center, Open-Meteo, USGS, OVSICORI, and the Red Sismológica Nacional. It also retrieves closed EONET events for historical context.

These requests are executed in parallel. Each source receives its own time budget so the application can process successful responses independently.

The original formats are converted into a shared DisasterAlert structure. This model includes the event identifier, source, category, title, level, date, coordinates, distance, magnitude, quality, details, original link, and additional reporting institutions.

The same normalized structure is used throughout the application. Event cards, maps, history, safety guidance, loved-one evaluation, and notifications can therefore work consistently regardless of the original source.

Seismic Integration and Deduplication

The seismic subsystem combines international and Costa Rican sources.

USGS contributes global earthquake information through its FDSN service. Gamma Alert calculates a regional geographic bounding box and requests earthquakes from the previous 30 days. OVSICORI provides a Costa Rican GeoJSON feed, while the Red Sismológica Nacional contributes RSS information about reviewed and felt earthquakes.

All three sources are queried in parallel and converted into a common seismic model. The merge process prioritizes RSN, followed by OVSICORI and USGS, allowing the application to preserve reviewed and locally felt information while retaining global coverage.

Multiple institutions may report the same earthquake. Gamma Alert identifies possible duplicates by comparing the normalized category, reporting time, source, and geographic distance.

For earthquakes, two reports can be grouped when they occur within approximately five minutes and 40 kilometers. The final record preserves one principal event and identifies the other institutions through an alsoReportedBy collection.

This prevents the interface from showing several cards for the same physical event while maintaining scientific traceability.

Geographic Relevance

Gamma Alert does not apply the same relevance rule to every hazard. Earthquakes, tsunamis, tropical cyclones, floods, volcanoes, rainfall, and other events have different geographic and temporal behaviors.

For earthquakes, the current rules consider magnitude 4 or greater within 50 kilometers, magnitude 5 or greater within 150 kilometers, magnitude 6.5 or greater within 400 kilometers, or a felt report within 60 kilometers.

Other hazards use their own combinations of distance, level, status, and date. Gamma Alert also assigns category-specific validity periods. When a report is no longer considered current, it can move into the history rather than disappearing.

The system distinguishes between an event that is recent and one considered ongoing. This allows the map to emphasize active situations while still preserving recent reports as regional context.

Interactive Map

We built the main map with MapLibre GL. It displays the user’s location, active events, historical events, hazard categories, loved ones, and contextual proximity areas.

Users can choose between a standard CARTO Voyager map, a Sentinel-2 satellite view from EOX and Copernicus, and an OpenTopoMap terrain view. The selected map style is stored locally.

Each event is represented according to its hazard category. The map legend is generated dynamically from the data currently displayed.

Ongoing events can receive red and yellow proximity rings. For earthquakes, the ring size is calculated from magnitude using an exponential distance expression. Volcanoes, tropical systems, floods, heavy rain, and landslides use category-specific reference radii.

The rings provide visual context about proximity and scale. They are not presented as official impact boundaries.

Selecting an event opens information about its title, category, date, source, and status. When a loved one is associated with a relevant event, the map can focus directly on that person’s approximate area.

MapLibre is dynamically loaded after the principal page content. This improves the initial experience by allowing the location status and event information to appear before the heavier cartographic component is initialized.

History and Source Transparency

Gamma Alert combines completed alerts, earlier seismic reports, closed EONET events, and selected radar observations into a historical view.

Users can filter the history by category. The filters and event counts are generated from the current dataset. Each event preserves its date, distance, source, details, and original scientific link.

Compatible events can open the NISAR Surface Explorer with their location, date, category, and title already included. This connects the event-monitoring experience directly with surface observation.

The live-source panel shows which integrations responded, the number of reports retrieved, the newest report time, and how many events from each source are visible to the user.

Gamma Alert currently tracks nine source groups in its standard dashboard workflow. By making their status visible, we allow users to understand which institutions contributed to the current result and when the application updated its information.

Environmental Assessment

Gamma Alert provides a local environmental assessment through GET /api/assess.

The endpoint retrieves current thermal observations from NASA GIBS, observations from a comparison date, and climate information from NASA POWER. The requests are processed in parallel.

NASA GIBS provides thermal information through geospatial vector tiles. Gamma Alert calculates which tiles intersect the selected area, downloads and decodes them, extracts thermal points, removes duplicates, and calculates each point’s distance from the user.

NASA POWER provides daily precipitation, maximum temperature, relative humidity, and wind information. Gamma Alert calculates the rainfall accumulated over the previous 30 days, compares it with equivalent historical periods, estimates the rainfall percentile, and calculates the number of days since significant rain.

The environmental score combines direct thermal observations with climate conditions. The thermal component considers proximity and intensity. The climate component considers dryness, wind, and low humidity.

The final result is classified as low, moderate, high, or extreme. The response also contains its strongest contributing reasons, confidence, update time, and scientific sources, making the assessment explainable.

Loved Ones

One of Gamma Alert’s most important human-centered features is Loved Ones.

People are not only concerned about what is happening near them. They also want to know whether their parents, children, partners, or friends are close to an earthquake, flood, tropical cyclone, volcanic event, tsunami bulletin, or another relevant hazard.

A user can create a temporary invitation, assign a familiar name such as “Mom” or “Grandfather,” and share the link. When the other person accepts, they authorize Gamma Alert to use an approximate area for hazard evaluation. The relationship can also be reciprocal.

Gamma Alert evaluates current scientific reports around each connected person using the same event engine, geographic calculations, time windows, and hazard-specific rules used by the main dashboard.

When a relevant event is found, the application displays the loved one’s approximate area on the map and identifies the nearby hazard, distance, date, and scientific source.

The purpose is not continuous personal tracking. Gamma Alert uses an approximate geographic area to connect trusted relationships with relevant scientific information.

Family Risk Notifications

The Loved Ones feature is integrated with Gamma Alert’s Web Push system.

When a relevant event is detected near a connected person, Gamma Alert can send a notification containing the loved one’s alias and the nearby hazard. This notification can be received even when the main application is closed.

Selecting the notification opens Gamma Alert and focuses the map on the loved one’s approximate area.

Each device generates a random identifier and secret key. The complete secret remains on the device, while the server stores only its SHA-256 hash.

Invitation codes are generated with 128 bits of cryptographic randomness. They expire after 48 hours and can only be used once. Shared coordinates are rounded to approximately one-kilometer precision before being stored.

This functionality transforms scientific monitoring into family awareness. It connects Earth observation and hazard information with the people users care about most.

Notifications and Progressive Web App

Gamma Alert supports notifications both inside the application and through the device’s operating system.

While the page is open, new relevant event identifiers can produce in-app notification cards containing the title, source, distance, and details.

For background notifications, the browser registers a service worker and creates an encrypted Web Push subscription. The subscription includes a secure HTTPS endpoint, encryption keys, language preference, approximate location, and optional device association.

A protected scheduled process loads subscriptions, groups nearby locations into geographic cells, evaluates current events, checks previously delivered records, and sends localized notifications.

The same cycle can evaluate a user’s location and the approximate locations of their loved ones. Delivered events are recorded to prevent repeated messages.

Gamma Alert’s web manifest defines its name, icons, theme colors, start URL, and standalone display mode. Compatible browsers can install the platform and open it similarly to a native application.

Safety Guidance

Gamma Alert includes contextual safety guidance for earthquakes, tsunamis, tropical systems, floods, heavy rain, volcanic activity, and fires.

The guidance is connected to the selected event. The interface presents the event title, source, date, distance, and relevant details alongside the recommendations.

Gamma Alert preserves links to the original scientific publications and official reference resources. The platform is designed as an educational and situational-awareness tool and does not replace instructions issued by authorized emergency-management institutions.

Bilingual and Accessible Experience

Gamma Alert supports Spanish and English throughout its main experience.

The selected language affects navigation, event categories, dates, source labels, safety information, invitations, loved-one status, radar explanations, and push notifications. The preference is stored locally and can also be represented in the page URL.

The interface uses semantic headings, keyboard-compatible controls, visible labels, translated map descriptions, and reduced-motion support. Colors are accompanied by text so information does not depend on color alone.

The layout adapts to phones, tablets, and desktop computers. Event lists can expand incrementally, radar acquisitions are presented through a scrollable timeline, and map controls remain available on smaller screens.

Demonstration Mode

Natural disasters do not occur on demand, but a project demonstration must show how the application responds.

Gamma Alert includes a clearly marked simulation mode for earthquakes, tsunamis, tropical systems, floods, volcanic events, fires, and combined scenarios.

Simulated events use the same data structure and interface components as real reports. They appear in event cards, map markers, proximity rings, safety guidance, and notifications while remaining clearly identified as simulations.

The application also includes a test-notification action. This allows judges and users to examine the notification experience without waiting for a new scientific event.

Technical Architecture

Gamma Alert is implemented as an integrated Next.js application. The interface and server-side APIs share TypeScript data models, allowing event structures to remain consistent throughout the system.

The principal technologies are Next.js 16.4.6, React 19.3, TypeScript 5.9, Tailwind CSS 4.3, MapLibre GL 6.18, SWR 2.5, Zod 4.6, Turf 7.4, Vitest 5.1, Node.js 22, and pnpm 11.

The browser manages interaction, map rendering, local preferences, NISAR image comparison, and notification permissions. The server validates input, protects credentials, retrieves external information, applies geographic and temporal rules, and returns structured JSON.

The principal internal services include /api/events, /api/assess, /api/alerts, /api/overlays, /api/nisar/search, /api/nisar/browse, /api/links/*, /api/push/subscribe, /api/push/cron, and /api/health.

Supabase stores the persistent information needed for devices, approximate locations, invitations, trusted relationships, push subscriptions, and notification records.

Performance and Resilience

Gamma Alert uses parallel source requests, explicit timeouts, controlled caching, and source isolation.

External services are queried with Promise.allSettled, allowing every successful source to contribute even when another source does not respond.

Current events use short cache periods because their information changes frequently. Environmental information uses a five-minute shared cache, geographic overlays use a 30-minute cache, NISAR searches use a six-hour cache, and immutable radar preview images can be cached for one week.

The internal in-memory cache supports up to 200 entries. Simultaneous requests for the same data can reuse one in-progress promise instead of creating duplicate external calls.

The frontend uses SWR to refresh current events every 30 seconds and revalidate selected information when the user returns to the application.

MapLibre is loaded dynamically, NISAR thumbnails use lazy loading, and the radar-image memory cache is limited to four images or 32 MiB.

Security and Privacy

All public endpoints validate their inputs before processing them. Latitude, longitude, radius, dates, device credentials, invitation codes, image identifiers, and push subscriptions are checked with Zod or strict format rules.

Scientific-service credentials and application secrets remain on the server.

The NISAR image service accepts only recognized GCOV collections and granule names that match the expected NASA format. It restricts redirect destinations, allows only secure cross-origin redirects, limits file size, applies timeouts, and verifies the PNG file signature.

Device secrets are stored as hashes, and authentication comparisons are timing-safe. Invitation codes are random, temporary, and single-use.

Locations used for Loved Ones and Web Push are stored with approximately one-kilometer precision. This provides enough context for regional hazard evaluation without storing the full precision of the original browser location.

Quality Assurance

The repository includes automated tests for alert rules, source parsers, geographic calculations, NISAR searches, SAR image processing, study navigation, invitations, device authentication, notification payloads, API behavior, and interface components.

Vitest runs the TypeScript and React tests. ESLint verifies code quality, while the production build confirms that Next.js can compile the application and its server routes.

The project’s automated workflow runs linting, tests, and the production build using Node.js 22 and pnpm.

Current Scientific Scope

The current radar comparison uses public eight-bit NISAR previews. It compares apparent HH brightness rather than calibrated gamma-naught or sigma-naught backscatter.

Radar response can change because of water, soil moisture, wind, vegetation, roughness, geometry, and acquisition conditions. Speckle and preview processing can also influence visual differences.

Gamma Alert therefore presents the current comparison as an exploratory surface-change visualization. Its results are designed to support observation and investigation rather than automatically classify damage.

The next scientific phase would use calibrated GCOV data, logarithmic intensity ratios, combined HH and HV features, and multi-date time series. Interferometric products and phase analysis would be required to study centimeter-scale ground deformation.

Impact

Gamma Alert creates value at the individual, family, educational, and community levels.

For individuals, it centralizes scientific reports and explains their geographic relationship with the user. For families, it extends awareness to trusted contacts. For students and educators, it connects real events with remote sensing, climate science, cartography, radar, and data processing.

For communities, the project demonstrates how NASA data can move beyond a scientific catalog and become part of an understandable public experience.

NASA EONET supports event monitoring and history. NASA GIBS contributes thermal observations. NASA POWER provides climate context. NASA CMR enables product discovery. NISAR supports surface comparison, and NASA Worldview provides optical context.

The project’s main innovation is not one isolated dataset. It is the connection among natural events, personal location, surface observations, scientific interpretation, and family communication.

Access to the Project

The public application is available at Gamma Alert.

The source code is available in the Gamma Alert GitHub repository.

Judges do not need to create an account. They can use the example location, grant location access, or activate the built-in demonstration mode.

To run the project locally, Node.js 22 and pnpm are required. From the web directory, dependencies can be installed with pnpm install, and the development environment can be started with pnpm dev.

Conclusion

With Gamma Alert, we built more than a natural-hazard map. We created an integrated system that retrieves scientific information, validates and standardizes it, calculates its geographic relevance, connects it with NISAR observations, and presents the result through an accessible application.

Gamma Alert combines a multi-hazard dashboard, event history, source transparency, environmental assessment, interactive maps, radar timelines, before-and-after comparisons, safety guidance, bilingual support, Loved Ones, Progressive Web App installation, and background notifications.

Its central idea remains simple: alerts tell us that something happened; NISAR helps us explore what happened to the surface.

By connecting those two perspectives, Gamma Alert transforms specialized scientific information into a tool for education, preparedness, family awareness, and community resilience.
